name: manual_e4c4c9
claim:
Two real security bugs found and fixed in diazMelgarejo/Claude-Desktop-LLM PR #1 (branch 2026-08-29-canonical-typescript-modernization, commits cb082af and 9a8c063), both worth auditing for in any v2/oramasys-org port of the same patterns, since this repo is TypeScript and forking into oramasys/* will involve re-deriving or re-porting this logic again.

(1) src/tools/handlers.ts's selectProvider() treated an omitted provider and an invalid supplied provider identically -- both silently fell through to ctx.config.activeProvider, so { provider: "invalid" } on any provider-selecting tool (e.g. local_llm_query) ran against activeProvider instead of erroring. Reachable despite the MCP tool JSON schemas declaring provider: { enum: ["ollama","lmstudio"] } for every such tool -- schema hints describe intent to well-behaved clients but the server had no independent enforcement between receiving a raw tool-call request and dispatching to handleToolCall. Fixed with one validation gate at the shared call site before selectProvider, covering every provider-selecting tool through the same switch statement. General lesson for any MCP tool server: never treat a declared JSON-schema enum as the actual enforcement boundary -- validate server-side independently, at the one shared dispatch point if the codebase has one, not per-tool.

(2) src/policy/endpoint-policy.ts's validateAndPin() computed addressIsLoopback = isLoopbackAddress(resolvedIp) || isLoopbackHostname(hostname) and skipped ALL of ALLOW_REMOTE_LLM/ALLOWED_LLM_HOSTS/HTTPS enforcement whenever this was true -- meaning a hostname that merely resolves to 127.0.0.1 via DNS got FULL loopback trust, identical to a hostname the caller directly wrote as "localhost" or "127.0.0.1". Concretely exploitable: an attacker who controls DNS for their own domain (they always do, for domains they own) can point it at 127.0.0.1 and get complete bypass of every remote-endpoint protection with zero allowlisting and zero HTTPS requirement, because the connection is pinned to the resolved IP (closing the classic DNS-rebinding TOCTOU gap) but the original attacker-chosen hostname is preserved for the Host header/TLS SNI -- this is a real security-boundary bypass, not cosmetic. There is no legitimate case where a genuinely-remote, allowlisted, HTTPS endpoint should ever resolve to loopback. Fixed with isDirectLoopbackSpecification(): true only for a recognized loopback name or a literal loopback IP the caller wrote directly, never based on a DNS lookup result; a hostname that is not itself loopback but resolves there is now rejected unconditionally, before any allow/allowlist/HTTPS check can permit it.

The comparative architecture finding, more consequential than either individual fix: this TypeScript file's own doc comment says it "mirrors Perpetua-Tools' src/utils/ssrf_pinned_adapter.py," but checking that actual Python file (and its SSOT deny predicate in src/utils/ssrf_fetch_policy.py) shows a fundamentally different, more robust design -- _is_denied_ip checks addr.is_loopback (Python's own ipaddress module property) on the ACTUAL RESOLVED address as one of several uniformly-denied ranges (loopback/private/link-local/CGNAT/multicast/reserved), with an explicit, separate allowlist mechanism layered on top for legitimate local-LLM use, and has NO hostname-string-based shortcut anywhere. The TypeScript port introduced a hostname-string classification path (isLoopbackHostname checking for "localhost"/"*.localhost") that grants automatic trust BEFORE uniformly checking the resolved address's actual range, and that architectural divergence from the original pattern is exactly where this vulnerability was introduced during the port. Bulk-remediation implication for v2: when forking or re-deriving this pattern into oramasys/* repos, audit for this specific divergence class -- "does the port classify by resolved-address-range uniformly (safe), or does it grant early trust based on the hostname string before resolution (unsafe)" -- in any language, not just re-copy the TypeScript file's current logic and assume it matches the canonical Python pattern.

decisions.notes: Direct instruction to document for v2/oramasys bulk remediation before CI finished -- two real, verified security fixes plus a more consequential comparative-architecture finding (the TS port diverged from the canonical Python pattern it claims to mirror, which is exactly where the vulnerability was introduced) worth checking systematically across future ports.

rationale: Direct instruction to document for v2/oramasys bulk remediation before CI finished -- two real, verified security fixes plus a more consequential comparative-architecture finding (the TS port diverged from the canonical Python pattern it claims to mirror, which is exactly where the vulnerability was introduced) worth checking systematically across future ports.
